nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name: Gulf pipefish
Scientific Name: Syngnathus scovelli

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Kingdom: Animalia
	Phylum: Chordata
	Class: Actinopterygii
	Order:  Gasterosteiformes
	Family: Syngnathidae

Other Common Names - Scovell's pipefish, pez pipa del Golfo

Note:	Reference for Scientific Name (Evermann and Kendall, 1896).
	Reference for Classification (Robins et al.1991)

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial: No commercial value.
Recreational:  Has some popularity as an aquarium fish (2390; 788).
Ecological Role:  One of the most ubiquitous estuarine seagrass/drift algal species within the Indian River Lagoon and therefore, plays a significant role in invertebrate grazing (993).  Syngnathid consumption of harpacticoid provide evidence that a fish-copepod link is integral to seagrass ecosystem function (2396).  Due to the abundance and small size gulf pipefish undoubtedly serve as prey for estuarine predators.
Indicator:   Syngnathus scovelli is dependent on aquatic vegetation such as seagrass and drift algae (2390;  2395; 2372).  Reduction in gulf pipefish population could indicate the loss of vegetation.

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  Along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts of Florida to southern Texas, Yucatan, Belize to Panama, Venezuela, parts of Brazil, and in freshwater habitats in west Florida, the St. Johns River, and Louisiana (2372; 2397; 2388; 2390; ).
Within Study Area: Found throughout the Indian River Lagoon but, conspicuously absent from freshwater tributaries to the Lagoon where it is replaced by Microphis brachyurus lineatus (848, 2391, 993; 2392; 2393; 2344; 2390; 2215).
Life Mode: Syngnathus scovelli is a euryhaline pipefish found in vegetated areas. Syngnathus scovelli is the most abundant pipefish found along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts of Florida (581; 2372; 664; 887; 2388; 2344; 2390; 993).   Syngnathus scovelli shares a unique behavior along with other syngnathids in that the male carries fertilized eggs in a brood pouch (327; 2390).
Mobility and Migration: Limited or localized movement and dispersal possibly associated with drift algae (2395).  Males with full brood pouches may move away from the females and non-brooding males (2397).

nodes.title: Habitat Type
nodes.body: Mostly associated with vegetation at  depths less than 6.1 m.  In estuarine areas associated with seagrass and algal bottoms, and principally away from ocean inlets in the Indian River Lagoon (2390; 2395; 993). Except along the east central coast of Florida,  Syngnathus scovelli occurs in freshwater and exhibits  a high degree  of association with Vallisneria, Spartina, Najas, Ruppia, and various other freshwater vegetation (2372; 2394; 2397; 2391; 2392; 2393).

nodes.title: Physical/Chemical
nodes.body: Syngnathus scovelli is a euryhaline species found from 0-56 ppt, though the Indian River lagoon population does not occur at salinities below 14 ppt (2372; 2397; 2389; Gilmore, unpublished data). Joseph (1957) and Brown (1972) showed a relationship of increased snout length of populations in low salinity.  Temperature ranges have been recorded from 10 - 36 C (581; 887; 2390).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode: Gonochoristic, oviparous,  iterparous, external fertilization possible during oviposition in male brood pouch.
Mating/Spawning: The female deposits the eggs in the male brood pouch located on the ventral side.  Brown (1972) recorded a maximum of 175 eggs in a pouch, with an average of 55.6 eggs per pouch.  The eggs are carried in two-four rows in the brood pouch, depending upon the size of the brood.  Brood size can increase with increase with fish size. Breder and Rosen (1966) observed in a congeneric species, that as the eggs are deposited in the pouch, fertilization takes place.  Spawning has been documented to occur year round in the Cedar Key population (581; 2388), and is considered a year round spawner in most of Florida, including the Indian River Lagoon (2372; 664; 887).  The males are capable of carrying another brood after parturition and producing up to 20 broods a year (2394; 1915; 2397; 2388; 2390)
Fecundity: A 87 mm female contained 94 eggs and a 121 mm female contained 143 mature eggs (2390).

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg:  Fertilized eggs are 0.9 - 1.3 mm in diameter. Brood pouch incubation time, 11-15 days (2394; 2388).
Larvae:  Larvae in brood pouch reach 12 - 15 mm TL before parturition (2394; 2397; 2388).
Juvenile:  Juvenile stage is from 12 - 60 mm TL in males and 12 - 80 mm TL in females (2390).
Adult: The size for sexual maturity differs for males and females.  The males mature in as early as six months at 60 mm TL.  Mature males develop a brood pouch on the ventral side in the form of fleshy ridges.  Most males exceed 90 mm TL.  Females mature at 80 mm TL are larger than males and exceed 100 mm TL.  Large females can reach 183 mm TL but rarely exceed 165 mm TL (2394; 2388; 2390).  The life span of adults is from one to three years (2397; 2388).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: The digestive tract of Syngnathus scovelli is specialized for a carnivorous diet.  The small tubular, terminal mouth restricts the size of organisms that can be captured by suction (2388).   Syngnathids are solitary cryptic  epibenthic  neritic and epibenthic suction  feeding microconsumers, which prey principally on copepods and amphipods  (993). Syngnathus scovelli is a diurnal carnivore with a diet consisting mainly of microcrustaceans, insect larvae and pupae, gastropods and even hatchling pipefish (581; 2372; 2394; 2388; 2387; 2396).   There is a ontogenic shift in food items consumed, as specimens under 70 mm TL feed mostly on copepods, while specimens 70-100 mm TL transition from planktonic food items to organisms living on seagrasses (2388; 2396).  Syngnathus scovelli over 100 mm TL feed mainly on amphipods (2388; 2390).

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body:
Predation:  One of the most ubiquitous estuarine seagrass/drift algal species within the Indian River Lagoon and therefore, plays a significant role in invertebrate grazing (993).  Syngnathid consumption of harpacticoid provide evidence that a fish-copepod link is integral to seagrass ecosystem function (2396).  Due to the abundance and small size gulf pipefish undoubtedly serve as prey for estuarine predators.
Factors influencing populations:  Syngnathus scovelli is dependent on aquatic vegetation such as seagrass and drift algae (2390;  2395; 2372).  Reduction in gulf pipefish population could indicate the loss of vegetation.
